lines.text: When my granddad died, splitting up his estate was basically a CrossFit workout.
Four hundred vinyl records.
Heavy as lead.
Taking three trips in the estate car just to get them to my house.
But you knew exactly where you stood!
He bought them, he owned them, boom, they were ours.
Contrast that with my mate Tom.
Tom's dad died a few months ago.
And look, Tom's dad was a legend, we miss him, this is not about grief.
This is about the absolute, farcical, administrative nightmare of modern life.
One of those days where the universe just points at you and laughs.
See, Tom's dad was a proper first-generation digital native.
Had a massive Steam library.
Thousands of pounds worth of games.
Tom's the executor, wants to do the right thing, decides to pass the games down to his teenage nephew.
So Tom emails the platform.
Here's the death certificate, lads. Let's transfer the account.
What do they do?
Bam.
Gone.
Vaporized.
"Licenses expire upon death, sir."
Account permanently closed.
In trying to be a good guy and do the right thing, Tom legally incinerated his nephew's inheritance in about four seconds.
Well done, Tom.
Slightly bruised, he moves on to the financial stuff.
Dad was into crypto.
Left behind a hardware wallet with a decent chunk of change on it.
But Tom needs the twenty-four word seed phrase.
Dad kept a backup in a secure email.
Smart!
So Tom sits at the PC, types in the password, hits enter.
Screen blinks.
"Please enter the six-digit code sent to your mobile device."
You can physically see the cold sweat form on Tom's neck.
Because Tom is a highly efficient executor.
His very first act, yesterday morning, was calling the telecom provider to cancel his dad's phone contract.
SIM card? Dead.
Number? Deactivated.
That two-factor authentication chain? Smashed to pieces.
He's not just locked out of the crypto.
He's locked out of the cloud.
A decade of family photos, videos, memories, suddenly sealed behind an impenetrable cryptographic blast door.
Panicking, Tom goes to the family solicitor.
You know the type.
Lovely old boy.
Still dictates onto mini-cassettes.
Smells like mahogany and dust.
Tom sits there raving about cryptographic lock-outs, severed two F A loops, evaporated software licenses...
and the solicitor just nods, adjusts his glasses, and goes,
"Right then. I shall write a stern letter to Mister Apple."
It's hilarious.
But then you stop laughing, and you realize...
we are so screwed.
For years, M I five and the police have been crying about this!
End-to-end encryption.
Unbreakable codes.
Tech companies refusing backdoors.
But now?
That military-grade encryption has finally come home to roost.
It's no longer just stopping terrorists.
It's stopping grieving families from getting the photos from last year's Christmas dinner!
We spent twenty years letting tech companies terrify us into building these unassailable digital fortresses to keep out the hackers.
But we forgot to build a front door for the people we leave behind.
We didn't build digital homes.
We built digital tombs.
So here we are, rushing to digitize our entire existence.
Are we seriously prepared to be the first generation in human history that leaves absolutely nothing behind,
just because our grieving kids couldn't pass a CAPTCHA proving they know what a crosswalk looks like?
Honestly, if I get hit by a bus tomorrow, forget the digital lawyers.
I'm having my twenty-four word crypto seed phrase laser-engraved, one letter at a time, across all four hundred of my granddad's vinyl records!
If my family wants my digital legacy, they're going to have to earn it the old-fashioned way,
three trips in the estate car and a double hernia.
